       NOTICE OF INTERVENTION AND PRELIMINARY COMMENTS OF THE
              NEW YORK STATE PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION


                                 NOTICE OF INTERVENTION

       The New York State Public Service Commission (“NYSPSC”) hereby submits its timely

Notice of Intervention in Docket No. EL26-69-000 pursuant to 18 C.F.R. §385.214 (Rule 214 of

the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's (Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure), and

the Commission’s June 18, 2026, Notice of Institution of Section 206 Proceeding and Refund

Effective Date. The NYSPSC is an executive regulatory agency of the sovereign State of New

York with jurisdiction to regulate rates and charges for the sale of electric energy to consumers

within the State, and participates in these proceedings as of right, pursuant to federal authorization

via the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) and the Commission’s implementing regulations. The

NYSPSC is a State Commission as defined in section 3(15) of the FPA, 16 U.S.C. §796(15), and

18 C.F.R. §1.101(k). Accordingly, pursuant to Rule 214(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of
 Practice and Procedure, the NYSPSC is entitled to intervene as a party in this proceeding as a

matter of right. 1

                                PRELIMINARY COMMENTS

        The NYSPSC recognizes the nascent stage of this proceeding and that subsequent filings

directed by the Commission will shape the course of the Commission’s deliberations, including

the New York Independent System Operator, Inc.’s (“NYISO”) “informational report on any

proposals under consideration in its stakeholder process to address the issue of resource adequacy

to serve new large loads.” 2 While the Commission has directed this inquiry on resource adequacy

to the NYISO, the NYSPSC is the primary entity responsible for ensuring the adequacy of

 generation resources in New York. As the Commission correctly notes, “states have exclusive

authority over resource planning and the generation mix within their boundaries” 3 and further, to

determine “which generation facilities are sited and allowed to serve co-located load.” 4

Accordingly, any proposals to address the issue of resource adequacy, as the Commission requests

to be identified in the informational report, 5 would concern the NYSPSC’s fundamental

responsibilities and jurisdiction.

       As the NYISO and stakeholders may consider potential approaches for planning adequate

generation to serve load, the NYSPSC is prepared to engage in discussions to develop solutions

that reflect the State’s authority and statutory mandates.        Unlike a multi-state Regional

Transmission Organization with competing state interests, New York, whose boundaries are

coextensive with the NYISO’s operational control area, is well positioned to address any resource

adequacy issues that may arise. The Commission should be assured that the NYSPSC takes the

matter of resource adequacy as a paramount responsibility and will take appropriate steps to ensure

all load in the State is served in a reliable manner, while maintaining affordability. The NYSPSC

has a long history of taking such action and, for example, initiated a proceeding recently in

December 2025 to address potential reliability needs in New York City, recognizing future needs

that were identified by the NYISO, as well as by Consolidated Edison Company of New York,

Inc. 6 Moreover, the NYSPSC routinely exercises its jurisdiction over reliability standards and

       With respect to the interconnection of large loads to the electric grid, the NYSPSC

commenced a proceeding in February 2026 focused, in part, on reviewing the planning and

interconnection processes, cost-allocation mechanisms, rate impacts, and tariff structures relating

to the integration of large loads within the State’s electric utility systems. 8 This State initiative

may examine opportunities to modernize interconnection processes, enhance transparency around

required grid upgrades, and improve cost predictability for projects.

       The NYSPSC appreciates the Commission’s acknowledgment that developing provisions

for the successful interconnection and service of large loads implicates the interests and authority

of New York State, and that it will therefore “respect the cooperative federalism approach

established under the FPA.” 9 This acknowledgment should provide the foundation to address

concerns raised by the Commission, as well as matters of importance within the States’ purview.
